A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SABRE-FL study and provide comparable main text and appendices. Although v2 visibly clips Algorithm 1 and Figure 6, their underlying content remains recoverable from the PDF and matches v1; these are layout defects rather than missing comparison evidence.

before.justification: v1 reports original federated backdoor and defense experiments in Tables 1–3, alongside embedding visualizations and ablations.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds further empirical evaluations in Appendix F, Tables 4–9, and Figure 9.

M1.justification: The learnable-trigger attack, frozen CLIP backbone, binary embedding detector, and rank-based client filtering remain unchanged. The alternative detector-training dataset and deliberately imperfect filtering are experimental variations, not revisions to the proposed algorithm.

E1.justification: The original dataset collection is retained, but its experimental roles expand. Appendix F reports downstream attack/defense evaluation on Caltech, previously used as the auxiliary detector-training dataset, and Table 9 uses Flowers as an alternative detector-training dataset.

E2.justification: Table 2 retains FedAvg without defense, Trimmed Mean, Median, Norm Bounding, and FLAME. The new experiments use existing no-defense comparisons. BadEncoder and contrastive poisoning are newly discussed related work, not newly evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: Appendix F introduces substantial additional evaluation protocols: five Dirichlet heterogeneity levels, half/double trigger strength, one/five trigger-optimization epochs, intentionally missed attackers, extra benign-client removal, and alternative auxiliary training. The original model, default settings, and accuracy metrics remain unchanged; these additions do not establish revisions or reruns of the original experiments.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained shot-count, attacker-fraction, client-scaling, and embedding analyses, Tables 4–9 test sensitivity to heterogeneity, attack strength, filtering errors, and auxiliary-dataset choice. Figure 9 adds learned-trigger visualizations. These substantially broaden the examination of the defense's assumptions and robustness.

E5.justification: v1's checklist explicitly acknowledges insufficient compute to rerun all experiments across seeds and report error bars, and promises later uncertainty experiments. v2 removes this disclosure with the checklist. Neither version supplies numerical uncertainty estimates or explicit repeated-run counts; additional runs cannot be inferred.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 and the original plotted results remain unchanged, while Tables 4–9 add substantial condition-specific findings. For example, Table 4 reports Aircraft backdoor accuracy of 89.6% with SABRE-FL versus 81.3% without defense at alpha = 0.1. Table 9 reports 0.2% versus 91.5% for Aircraft with a Flowers-trained detector. These are new evaluations, not improvements to the original scores.

T1.justification: The attack formalization, embedding-separation assumption, detector objective, client score, and generalization lemma are retained. The FedAvg equations become inline expressions and subsequent equations are renumbered; no substantive mathematical revision or new proof appears.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution statements, and conclusion retain the same claims about federated prompt-learning vulnerability, SABRE-FL's embedding-based defense, and superiority over four defenses across five datasets. The additional experiments do not redefine these central contributions.

C2.justification: The new Section 3.1 positioning paragraph explicitly justifies restricting evaluation to BadCLIP because of its compatibility with prompt tuning. Appendix F interprets its additions as supporting practical robustness and generalization. Existing limitations remain unchanged, including the now-outdated statement that client heterogeneity was not explicitly varied.

D1.justification: Appendix D.4 newly states that the detector file occupies a few megabytes. Removing the checklist also removes descriptions of supplemental code, instructions.txt, and modifications to the BadCLIP codebase. Both versions retain the future public-release promise, so an actual change in code availability is not established.

R1.justification: Section 3.1 adds a focused comparison with centralized and pretraining attacks, including new citations to BadEncoder by Jia et al. and contrastive poisoning by Carlini and Terzis. Existing BadCLIP references and the broader research positioning are retained.

P1.justification: Most prose and section order are preserved. v2 adds a positioning paragraph, shortens several passages, replaces the main experimental-settings subsection with an appendix pointer, adds Appendix F, and removes the NeurIPS checklist. Citations change from numbered to author-year style; the core narrative is not extensively rewritten.

P2.justification: v2 adds six tables and a trigger-visualization figure while reformatting and reflowing retained displays. Unlike v1, Algorithm 1 and Figure 6 extend beyond the visible page boundaries, and Figure 4's caption overlaps body text. These are substantial display and readability changes, although the original figure content is retained.

improvement.justification: Appendix F provides useful diagnostic evidence about assumptions left untested in v1, particularly heterogeneous clients, filtering mistakes, and auxiliary-dataset dependence. This modest empirical gain is tempered by failure cases not reconciled with the robustness discussion, the outdated Appendix A limitation, and new clipping of Algorithm 1 and Figure 6. Because the method and original evidence remain available, the added tests provide a limited net improvement despite these defects.
